question: A single core of a finite real tensor train is a real matrix whose rows are indexed by the left bond and whose columns are indexed by a composite label: an ordered pair of an emitted bit (two values) and a right-bond index (r values). To factorize this core, one reshapes that composite column label into a single flat column label and then performs a thin factorization in the flat coordinates. Explain (a) why the reshaping is a genuine bijection and what the flat label's size is, (b) why performing the factorization in flat coordinates and then relabeling the result back by the inverse reshaping produces valid factors of the original core, and (c) why the row-orthonormality of the orthonormal factor is unaffected by the relabeling. State the resulting inner (new left-bond) dimension.
reference_answer: (a) The composite column label ranges over all ordered pairs (bit, right-bond index) with the bit taking 2 values and the right-bond index taking r values. The set of such pairs has exactly 2 times r elements, and there is a fixed bijection between it and the flat label set {0,...,2r-1}; reshaping is simply applying this bijection, so no column is lost, duplicated, or merged. The flat label therefore has size 2r. (b) A thin factorization in flat coordinates writes the reshaped core as R times Q where Q has orthonormal rows. Relabeling the columns of Q back by the inverse bijection permutes/renames columns without changing any entry, so the matrix product R times (relabeled Q) reproduces the original core entry by entry: for each original column (bit, j) the entry equals the flat-coordinate entry at the image label, which the factorization already matches. Hence R and the relabeled Q are valid factors of the original core. (c) Row-orthonormality is the statement that Q times Q-transpose equals the identity, i.e. each pair of rows has the prescribed inner product summed over columns. Relabeling columns by a bijection only reorders the terms of that per-row-pair sum, and a finite sum is invariant under reindexing by a bijection, so the row-Gram matrix is unchanged; the relabeled Q still has orthonormal rows. The inner (new left-bond) dimension is the minimum of the original left bond and 2r, i.e. min(left bond, 2 * right bond).

rubric.criterion: States the composite (bit, right-bond) label is in bijection with a flat label of size 2r (2 bit-values times r right indices).
Explains that relabeling columns by the inverse bijection leaves entries unchanged, so R times the relabeled factor reproduces the original core.
Explains row-orthonormality survives because a finite column sum is invariant under bijective reindexing; states inner dimension min(left bond, 2*right bond).

assumptions: the core is a real matrix with composite column index (bit of 2 values, right bond of r values)
a thin factorization with orthonormal rows exists in flat coordinates
conventions: columns reshaped by a fixed finite-product bijection of size 2r
orthonormal rows means Q*Q-transpose = identity

Factorizing in flat coordinates and relabeling back reproduces the original core because column relabeling preserves entries and products.
Row-orthonormality is preserved because the per-row-pair column sum is invariant under bijective reindexing; inner dimension is min(left bond, 2*right bond).

difficulty.rationale: Requires understanding why a composite-to-flat column reshaping is a bijection and why matrix products and row-Gram sums are invariant under bijective reindexing.

question: During backward canonicalization of a finite real tensor train, a residual matrix R (left over from factorizing a later core) must be absorbed into the right bond of the preceding core A, where A emits one bit of two possible values and has a right-bond index. The absorption produces a new core whose entry at left index a and composite column (bit, j) is the sum over the old right-bond index b of A at (a, bit, b) times R at (b, j). Explain in matrix-slice terms what this absorption does to each of the two emitted-bit branches of A, and justify why it does not mix the two bit branches together. State the single slice identity that captures this.
reference_answer: View the core A, with the emitted bit fixed to a value, as an ordinary matrix called the bit-slice of A for that bit value: its rows are indexed by the left bond and its columns by the right bond. The absorption of R multiplies each such bit-slice on the right by R: the bit-value-0 slice of the absorbed core is the bit-value-0 slice of A times R, and the bit-value-1 slice of the absorbed core is the bit-value-1 slice of A times R. In other words absorption is just an independent right matrix multiplication performed within each emitted-bit branch. It cannot mix the two branches because the defining sum runs only over the old right-bond index b and carries the emitted bit through unchanged on both sides: the bit label of an output column equals the bit label fed in, and R acts only on the right-bond coordinate, never on the bit coordinate. The single identity that captures this is: the bit-b slice of (absorb A R) equals (the bit-b slice of A) times R, for each bit value b. This is why absorption changes bond dimensions on the right while preserving the bit structure the core emits.

States the slice identity: slice(absorb A R, b) = slice(A, b) * R for each bit value b.
Explains no bit-mixing: the sum is only over the right-bond index and the emitted bit is carried through unchanged.

R is a real matrix on the right-bond index
conventions: a bit-slice fixes the emitted bit and leaves an ordinary left-by-right matrix

Formally, slice(absorb A R, bit) = slice(A, bit) * R for each bit value.

question: A stencil coefficient is written in a small symbolic language whose expressions are built from rational constants, named symbols, and the operations addition, multiplication, and negation. Given an environment that assigns a rational number to each symbol name, the coefficient is turned into a concrete rational number by a single evaluation map. State how this map treats each of the five kinds of expression, and state precisely which algebraic structure the evaluation preserves (that is, which equalities relate the value of a compound expression to the values of its parts).
reference_answer: Evaluation sends a rational-constant expression to that same rational number; it sends a symbol to whatever rational the environment assigns to that symbol's name; and it is defined recursively on the three operations so that the value of a sum is the sum of the values, the value of a product is the product of the values, and the value of a negation is the negation of the value. In other words, for a fixed environment the evaluation map is a homomorphism of the symbolic coefficient algebra onto the rationals: it commutes with addition, with multiplication, and with negation, and it maps the constant symbols for 0 and 1 to the rationals 0 and 1. Consequently any symbolic identity built only from +, *, and negation holds for the evaluated rationals, which is exactly what lets symbolic stencil rows be manipulated before any numeric assignment is chosen.

rubric.criterion: States evaluation of constants (to themselves) and symbols (to the environment value).
States the three homomorphism identities: value of sum/product/negation equals sum/product/negation of values.
Identifies the map as a (ring/algebra) homomorphism onto the rationals, including 0 and 1 mapping correctly.

assumptions: the environment assigns a rational to every symbol name
conventions: coefficients are symbolic expressions over the rationals
evaluation is relative to a fixed environment

semantic_steps.claim: Constants evaluate to themselves and symbols to their assigned rational.
Evaluation commutes with addition, multiplication, and negation.

difficulty.rationale: Recall of a recursive evaluation and recognition of the homomorphism property.

question: A block-encoding unitary represents an operator that acts on the 2^n states of an n-qubit system register, using a auxiliary qubits. (a) What is the dimension of the square matrix representing the full unitary, and why? (b) The full index is a flattened combination of a signal/ancilla register and the system register; state which register is treated as the high-order (most significant) part of the index and which as the low-order part. (c) If one instead keeps the two registers explicit as an ordered pair (signal, system) and reads off the sub-matrix for one fixed value of the signal register, how does that sub-matrix relate to the sub-matrix obtained by projecting the single flattened unitary onto the same signal branch?
reference_answer: (a) The full unitary is a 2^(n+a) by 2^(n+a) matrix. The combined register has n + a qubits (n system qubits plus a auxiliary qubits), and a register of n+a qubits has 2^(n+a) basis states, so the unitary acting on all of them is a square matrix of that size. (b) The signal/ancilla register is the high-order (most significant) part of the flattened index and the system register is the low-order part; equivalently the flat index is signalIndex times (system dimension) plus systemIndex. (c) They are the same matrix. Taking the explicit product-register view of the flat unitary and then extracting the block for one fixed signal value yields exactly the same entries, position by position, as projecting the single flattened unitary onto that signal branch; the two descriptions are definitionally identical, so reasoning done in either view transfers to the other without any change of entries.

rubric.criterion: States the full dimension is 2^(n+a) and justifies it by the n+a combined qubits.
Identifies signal/ancilla as high-order and system as low-order in the flattened index.
States the explicit product-register branch equals the flattened block projection entry-for-entry.

a auxiliary qubits are used
conventions: signal/ancilla register is high-order, system register is low-order
flat index = signal * systemDim + system

The flat index places the signal register high-order and the system register low-order.

question: You are given r real column vectors in R^N that are orthonormal (each has unit length and distinct ones are orthogonal), presented as the columns of an N-by-r matrix V satisfying V-transpose times V equals the r-by-r identity. You are also given an arbitrary assignment that places these r columns into r distinct column positions among the N columns of a target N-by-N matrix (the positions need not be the first r columns, and need not be contiguous). Prove that there exists an N-by-N real orthogonal matrix U (U-transpose times U equals the N-by-N identity) whose columns at exactly those r prescribed positions are the given vectors. Make explicit each ingredient your argument relies on.
reference_answer: First, the hypothesis V-transpose times V = identity says exactly that the r columns of V form an orthonormal family of vectors in R^N; in particular the family has r elements and since an orthonormal family is linearly independent, r <= N. Second, the prescribed placement is an injection from the r column-labels into the N positions, so it merely relabels the same r orthonormal vectors at distinct physical positions without changing their inner products; the placed family is therefore still orthonormal. Third, in the N-dimensional inner-product space R^N, any orthonormal family can be extended to an orthonormal basis of the whole space (basis-extension / Gram-Schmidt completion); this produces N - r additional unit vectors orthogonal to each other and to the prescribed ones, filling the N - r unused positions. Fourth, assemble U by taking as its columns these N orthonormal vectors, with the prescribed vectors sitting at their assigned positions and the completion vectors at the remaining positions. Because all N columns are orthonormal, U-transpose times U is the identity, i.e. U is orthogonal, and by construction its columns at the prescribed positions are exactly the given vectors. Hence such a U exists. The essential ingredients are: (i) the equivalence between the identity equation and column-orthonormality, (ii) invariance of orthonormality under an injective relabeling of positions, and (iii) the orthonormal-basis extension theorem in a finite-dimensional inner-product space whose dimension equals the number of positions.

Argues the injective placement preserves orthonormality (relabeling distinct positions keeps inner products).
Invokes orthonormal-basis extension to fill the remaining N - r positions in R^N.
Assembles U, concludes orthogonality from all-columns-orthonormal and that prescribed columns match.

the placement of columns is an injection into the N positions
conventions: real matrices

question: Suppose r orthonormal real columns are placed at r distinct positions among the N columns of an orthogonal matrix, and suppose r < N so at least one column position is left free. The naive completion to an orthogonal matrix may land in the reflection family (determinant -1) rather than the rotation family (determinant +1). Prove that one can always repair the orientation so the final matrix has determinant exactly +1 while leaving every one of the r prescribed columns completely unchanged. Explain why the strict inequality r < N is exactly what makes the repair possible, and why the repair cannot in general be done when r = N.
reference_answer: Start from any orthogonal completion U whose prescribed columns are the given vectors. Because U is orthogonal, U-transpose U = I forces det(U)^2 = 1, so det(U) is either +1 or -1. If it is already +1 there is nothing to do. If it is -1, we fix it with a single-column sign flip at an unused position. Since r < N, the r prescribed positions do not exhaust the N columns, so there is at least one position, call it 'unused', that carries no prescribed column. Let S be the diagonal matrix that is the identity except for a -1 in the unused position. S is orthogonal (it is diagonal with entries +/-1, so S-transpose S = I) and det(S) = -1. Replace U by U*S. Then (U S)-transpose (U S) = S-transpose (U-transpose U) S = S-transpose S = I, so U*S is still orthogonal; and det(U S) = det(U) det(S) = (-1)(-1) = +1, so it is now a rotation. Crucially, right-multiplying by this diagonal S only rescales the single unused column by -1 and leaves every other column, in particular all r prescribed columns, exactly as it was. Hence the prescribed data is preserved and the orientation is corrected. The strict inequality r < N is essential because the repair needs a column that is NOT prescribed to absorb the sign flip; if r = N every column is prescribed, flipping any of them would change the required data, and indeed a fully prescribed orthonormal frame with determinant -1 simply cannot be reoriented to +1 without altering a prescribed column, so no determinant-+1 completion that fixes all N columns exists.

rubric.criterion: Derives det(U) in {+1,-1} from orthogonality (det squared = 1).
Uses r < N to secure an unused column position and builds the diagonal sign-flip S there.
Shows U*S stays orthogonal and has determinant +1 (product of determinants).
Shows right-multiplication by S changes only the unused column, preserving all prescribed columns, and explains the r = N obstruction.

question: In a finite complex matrix backend, acting with an operator on a computational-basis state (a vector with a single 1 at one position and 0 elsewhere) returns the corresponding column of the operator. Using only this fact and the linearity of matrix-vector multiplication, prove that acting with an operator A on the two-term superposition a*|left> + b*|right>, where |left> and |right> are two basis states, gives a*(column left of A) + b*(column right of A), and that the amplitude read at output row k equals a*A[k,left] + b*A[k,right]. Explain why this means a block-encoding or state-preparation witness never needs to reconstruct the whole matrix-vector product: only two named columns, or two named entries, are ever required.
reference_answer: Matrix-vector multiplication is linear in the vector argument: for scalars a, b and vectors u, w we have A(a*u + b*w) = a*(A u) + b*(A w), and A(c*u) = c*(A u). Apply this with u = |left> and w = |right>. By the basis-column fact, A|left> is exactly the 'left' column of A and A|right> is exactly the 'right' column of A. Therefore A(a*|left> + b*|right>) = a*(A|left>) + b*(A|right>) = a*(column left of A) + b*(column right of A). Reading the k-th coordinate of both sides and using that the k-th coordinate of the 'j' column of A is the entry A[k,j], the output amplitude at row k is a*A[k,left] + b*A[k,right]. Consequently, to certify what an operator does to any two-term superposition it suffices to inspect the two named columns (vector form) or, for a single output amplitude, just the two named matrix entries (scalar form). No sum over all basis states or full reconstruction of the matrix-vector product is needed; the sparsity of the input collapses the computation to exactly the terms whose input amplitude is nonzero. This is why finite preparation and block-encoding witnesses are stated and checked column-wise or entry-wise rather than by rebuilding a dense product.

question: Two proof styles are commonly used to certify that a flattened signal-system unitary block-encodes a target operator on the system register at a fixed 'clean' signal value. Style A proves a pointwise equality: the matrix block obtained by projecting the unitary onto that clean signal branch equals the target matrix entry by entry. Style B proves an action statement: for every clean-signal basis input and every clean-signal output row, the amplitude the unitary produces equals the corresponding target matrix entry. Prove that these two styles are logically equivalent, by first showing the single bridging identity that the clean-input/clean-output amplitude of the unitary equals exactly one entry of the projected block.
reference_answer: The bridge is: for a fixed clean signal value and any output and input system indices, the amplitude obtained by feeding the clean-signal basis input into the unitary and reading the clean-signal output row equals exactly the (output, input) entry of the projected block of the unitary at that signal value. This holds because acting on a basis ket selects a column (the basis-column fact), and selecting the clean-output coordinate of that column is by definition the same entry that the signal-branch projection reads off; so the amplitude and the projected-block entry are literally the same number for every output and input. Now prove the equivalence. (Style A implies Style B) Assume the projected block equals the target entrywise. Fix any output and input. By the bridge the clean-input/clean-output amplitude equals the projected-block (output,input) entry, which by assumption equals the target (output,input) entry; so the action statement holds for every output and input. (Style B implies Style A) Assume the action statement holds for all outputs and inputs. Fix any output and input; the projected-block (output,input) entry equals, by the bridge, the clean-input/clean-output amplitude, which by assumption equals the target (output,input) entry; so the projected block equals the target entrywise. Since each direction follows from the single bridging identity applied at an arbitrary (output, input) pair, the two certification styles are equivalent. (Linearity further extends the basis action to arbitrary system inputs, and any orthogonal failure branch is separate unitarity evidence rather than a competing block contract.)

rubric.criterion: States and justifies the bridge: clean-input/clean-output amplitude = projected-block entry (via basis-ket selects a column).
Proves Style A => Style B by applying the bridge at an arbitrary (output,input).
Proves Style B => Style A symmetrically.

question: Let V be a real N-by-r matrix whose columns are orthonormal, expressed by the identity V-transpose times V equals the r-by-r identity. (a) Prove the dimensional obstruction r <= N. (b) Suppose further that the strict inequality r < N holds and that the r columns are placed at r distinct positions among the N available column positions via an injective assignment from the r column-labels into the N positions. Prove that this assignment cannot be surjective, i.e. at least one of the N positions receives no prescribed column. Make the counting argument explicit and explain how these two facts together guarantee a spare position exists exactly when r < N.
reference_answer: (a) The identity V-transpose times V = identity says that for every pair of column labels the inner product of the corresponding columns is 1 when the labels agree and 0 when they differ; that is, the r columns form an orthonormal family in R^N. An orthonormal family is linearly independent: if a linear combination of the columns were zero, taking the inner product with each column in turn (using orthonormality) forces every coefficient to be zero. A linearly independent family in an N-dimensional vector space has at most N members, because its size cannot exceed the dimension. Hence r, the number of columns, satisfies r <= N. This is the isometry dimensional obstruction: an inner-product-preserving (isometric) linear map from R^r into R^N can exist only when r <= N. (b) The placement is an injective function e from the r column-labels into the N positions. Suppose, for contradiction, that e were also surjective. A surjection from a finite set of size r onto a finite set of size N forces the size of the target to be at most the size of the source, i.e. N <= r (a surjection cannot increase cardinality). But we assumed r < N, i.e. N > r, contradicting N <= r. Therefore e is not surjective: there exists at least one position in the N positions that is not in the image of e, i.e. an unused position receiving no prescribed column. Together: part (a) shows orthonormal columns can only exist when r <= N, and part (b) shows that in the strict regime r < N the injective placement always leaves a spare position. When instead r = N, the injection is a bijection and no spare position exists, which is precisely the boundary that distinguishes the two regimes.

Concludes r <= N because a linearly independent family has size at most the dimension (isometry obstruction).
Gives the counting contradiction: a surjection Fin r -> Fin N would force N <= r, contradicting r < N, so e is non-surjective.
Concludes a spare/unused position exists exactly in the strict regime r < N (and not when r = N).

question: When embedding a right-canonical tensor-train core into a larger fixed physical register by zero-padding its outputs, one claims the active clean-input columns remain orthonormal and that right-multiplication of the boundary stays mass-preserving. A reviewer argues: 'the padded core still satisfies core times core-transpose equals the identity on the physical register, so its rows are orthonormal and nothing changes'. Show by an explicit small example that the reviewer's blanket claim is false: padding generally destroys the ROW orthonormality relation even though it preserves the COLUMN orthonormality of the active clean-input columns. State precisely which relation survives padding and which does not, and why only the surviving one is used.
reference_answer: Take the simplest nontrivial case: a core whose matrix, after fixing the emitted bit, acts as the 1-by-1 identity (its single active row/column is the scalar 1), and pad its output into a physical register of dimension 2 by appending a zero output row. Writing the padded clean-input column as the 2-component vector (1, 0): the column relation (conjugate-transpose times itself) gives (1,0).(1,0) = 1, so the single active clean-input column is still a unit column orthonormal to the (absent) others. But the row relation (matrix times its own transpose on the physical register) now has rows (1,0) and (0,0): the second row is the zero vector, so the matrix-times-transpose is diag(1,0), NOT the 2-by-2 identity. Hence padding breaks 'rows orthonormal' (core*core-transpose = I fails) while keeping 'active clean-input columns orthonormal' (the column Gram matrix on active indices stays the identity). This is a general phenomenon: zero-padding adds all-zero output rows, and a matrix with a zero row can never satisfy matrix*matrix-transpose = I (that identity forces every row to have unit norm). What survives is the column isometry restricted to the active clean-input labels, because the extra padded output rows are identically zero and contribute nothing to the column inner products. The library therefore states the preserved property as orthonormality of the active clean-input columns after embedding, and uses only that; the naive 'rows stay orthonormal on the physical register' claim is false and is correctly avoided.

rubric.criterion: Gives a concrete small padded example (e.g. active block = [1], padded column (1,0) in a size-2 register).
Shows the row relation fails: a zero padded row makes core*core-transpose = diag(1,0) != I.
Shows the active-column relation survives: the clean-input column Gram matrix is still the identity.
States the general reason (a zero row cannot satisfy row-orthonormality) and that only the active-column isometry is used.

assumptions: the original core is right-canonical (orthonormal rows before padding)

question: The special-orthogonal completion result guarantees that prescribed orthonormal columns can be extended to a determinant-+1 orthogonal matrix WHENEVER the number of prescribed columns is strictly less than the ambient dimension. A student conjectures the strict inequality is just a technical convenience and that the result still holds when the prescribed columns already fill all the positions (number of prescribed columns equal to the ambient dimension). Give an explicit counterexample disproving the student's conjecture, and identify exactly which step of the strictly-fewer-columns argument has no analogue in the fully-prescribed case.
reference_answer: Work in dimension N = 2 with r = 2 prescribed columns, i.e. all columns prescribed. Let the two prescribed orthonormal columns be (1, 0) and (0, -1), placed at positions 1 and 2. They are orthonormal: each has unit length and they are orthogonal, so the matrix V = [[1,0],[0,-1]] satisfies V-transpose V = identity. The only orthogonal matrix whose columns at positions 1 and 2 are exactly these vectors is V itself, because every column is already dictated by the prescription; there is no free column to choose. But det(V) = (1)(-1) - 0 = -1, so V is a reflection, not a rotation, and it is the unique completion. Therefore no determinant-+1 orthogonal matrix has these prescribed columns, disproving the conjecture: the result genuinely fails when the prescribed columns fill all positions. The step with no analogue is the orientation-repair step. In the strictly-fewer-columns argument one selects an UNUSED column position and flips its sign to turn a determinant-(-1) completion into a determinant-(+1) one while leaving all prescribed columns untouched. When every position is prescribed there is no unused column to absorb the sign flip; any sign change or rotation would have to alter a prescribed column, which is forbidden. So the existence of a spare column, guaranteed only by the strict inequality (number of prescribed columns < ambient dimension), is exactly the ingredient that disappears, and with it the determinant-+1 guarantee.

rubric.criterion: Gives an explicit fully-prescribed orthonormal frame with determinant -1 (e.g. columns (1,0),(0,-1) in dimension 2).
Argues the completion is forced to be V itself with determinant -1, so no determinant-+1 completion exists.
Identifies the missing step as the sign-flip orientation repair, which needs an unused column available only when prescribed-count < dimension.

the conjecture drops the strict inequality and allows prescribed-count = dimension
conventions: real matrices

difficulty.rationale: A sharp boundary counterexample pinpointing why a hypothesis is necessary, not merely convenient.

question: A finite real tensor train is right-canonicalized by sweeping from the terminal bond backward, replacing each core by one with orthonormal rows while absorbing a residual into the preceding core. The active left bond dimension produced at each core obeys the exact backward recurrence: the new left bond is the minimum of (the current left bond) and (twice the next active bond). Using only this recurrence and the fact that the sweep never enlarges any bond, prove two boundary facts: (a) after canonicalization every core's left bond is at most its original left bond AND at most twice its next active bond; and (b) for a scalar-boundary chain whose terminal bond is forced to dimension one, the active bond immediately before the terminal bond is at most two. Explain where the factor of two comes from.
reference_answer: The factor of two comes from the physical bit each core emits: a core carries an emitted bit of dimension 2 together with its right bond, so when it is reshaped and factorized the inner (new left) dimension cannot exceed the number of columns of the reshaped bit/right-bond block, which is 2 times the right (next active) bond. The factorization also cannot increase the row count, so the new left bond cannot exceed the original left bond either. Hence the new left bond is at most the minimum of the original left bond and twice the next active bond, which is exactly the stated recurrence. (a) Reading the recurrence directly: new left bond = min(original left bond, 2 * next active bond) <= original left bond, and <= 2 * next active bond. Both inequalities hold simultaneously because the minimum of two quantities is at most each of them. So every canonicalized core's left bond is bounded by both its original left bound and twice its next active bond. (b) Consider a chain of length one over a scalar (dimension-one) terminal boundary: the single core's right/next active bond is the terminal bond, which is forced to be dimension one. Apply the bound from (a) to this core: its left bond is at most 2 times its next active bond = 2 * 1 = 2. Therefore the active bond immediately preceding a dimension-one terminal bond is at most two. Intuitively, once the chain has been squeezed down to a scalar output, the preceding bond can retain at most the two values the final emitted bit can distinguish, so its dimension cannot exceed two.

rubric.criterion: Explains the factor of two as the emitted bit of dimension 2 multiplying the right/next-active bond (reshape column count).
Derives (a): new left bond = min(original, 2*next) is at most each of the two quantities.
Derives (b): for a length-one chain with terminal bond 1 the preceding bond is at most 2*1 = 2.

assumptions: canonicalization follows the backward min(l, 2*m') recurrence

difficulty.rationale: Boundary reasoning from a min-recurrence to two simultaneous bounds and a concrete terminal specialization; genuine multi-node composition.
